Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
David has been a forester for thirty years, and for most of that time, the woods were the only place he felt truly competent. That all changed eight months ago, on a crisp autumn afternoon. He was operating the skidder, pulling felled logs up a steep grade, a task he’d performed thousands of times. Leo, a seasonal worker not much older than his own son, was spotting for him. The ground was softer than it looked after an overnight rain. David felt the machine lurch, a sudden, sickening slide to the left. In the split second it took him to correct, the log stack shifted. He remembers the crack of splintering pine and Leo’s shout, cut short. The weight of his experience, his mastery of the machine and the terrain, had vanished in an instant, replaced by the image of Leo pinned beneath the load.

In the months that followed, the forest became a hostile territory. His supervisor, trying to be helpful, assigned him to inventory duties on the flatter, safer plots. But even the physical proximity to the familiar woods was enough to bring on a cold sweat. He found he couldn’t work. The company eventually moved him to a desk, a gesture of kindness that felt like a confirmation of his failure. He was no longer the man who could read a landscape at a glance; he was the man who couldn’t be trusted with machinery. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. This conviction settled deep in his bones, a certainty that there was something intrinsically wrong with him, a fundamental flaw that had made the accident inevitable.

The memories are not just images; they are physical events. He can be standing in his own kitchen when, without warning, his body reenacts the moment. His hands will clench as if gripping the joysticks, the muscles in his back and shoulders seizing in the exact posture of bracing for the skidder’s impact. The sensation is often followed by a flash of white-hot rage directed entirely at himself—for his carelessness, for his arrogance in thinking he had the situation under control. Then comes the grief, a hollow, crushing weight for the life he altered. He thinks of Leo, who now walks with a permanent limp and can no longer do the work he loved. Seeing any young man with a similar build or a familiar gait can stop David in his tracks, his breath catching in his throat.

His sense of being a danger to others has bled out from the forest into the rest of his life. He feels he can’t rely on himself, not just at work, but anywhere. In a crowded grocery store, he watches other people with a hawk-like intensity, not because he fears they will harm him, but because he is terrified he will somehow harm them. He imagines tripping and sending an elderly woman tumbling, or bumping his cart into a child. He gives strangers a wide berth, his body tense, his mind calculating potential vectors of accidental harm. His wife, Sarah, notices he can never relax, even sitting on their own porch. He’s always scanning, listening, braced for a threat he can’t name but is certain originates within himself. Any sharp, unexpected pain in his own body—a twinge in his back when he lifts a bag of dog food—can catapult him back to the splintering sound of the logs and the feeling of utter, catastrophic failure.

David finally sought help after a visit from Leo a few weeks ago. The young man came to the house, leaning on his cane, and spoke with a forgiveness David felt he had no right to receive. After he left, David sat in his truck for an hour, overwhelmed by a grief so total it felt like annihilation. He realized he was not just living with a memory, but being erased by it. He is here now because the man he used to be is gone, and he is terrified that the broken, unreliable person who remains is all he will ever be again.

missing_explanations: The vignette describes the patient's fear of harming strangers, not a fear of being harmed by them. The patient is described as watching others closely and keeping his distance because he is 'terrified he will somehow harm them', which is the opposite of the reported symptom.
